How sound flows through our system

beginner · about 6 min · updated 2026-05-11

If you’ve ever wondered “what actually happens between someone singing into a mic and the sound coming out of the speakers,” this article is for you. Understanding the path the signal takes is the single most useful thing you can know — almost every troubleshooting decision starts with “where in the chain is the problem?”

The chain, in plain English

A sound signal travels through our system in this order:

  1. Source — A voice or instrument makes a sound.
  2. Microphone or DI box — Converts the sound into a tiny electrical signal.
  3. XLR cable (or 1/4” cable) — Carries the tiny signal to the mixer.
  4. Mixer input — TRIM (also called GAIN) — Boosts the tiny signal up to a “good” level for the rest of the board.
  5. Channel processing — EQ, compression, etc. (We usually leave these alone.)
  6. Channel fader — How loud this channel is in the main mix.
  7. Master fader — How loud the overall mix is.
  8. Amplifier (if separate) — Boosts the signal one more time to drive the speakers.
  9. Speaker cable — Carries the now-loud signal to the speakers.
  10. Speakers — Convert the electrical signal back into sound.

If you can’t hear something, the question is always: which step is the problem? Test in order:

  • Is the mic on / battery good? (step 2)
  • Is the cable plugged in at both ends? (step 3)
  • Is the TRIM up? (step 4)
  • Is the channel UNMUTED and the fader UP? (step 6)
  • Is the master fader UP? (step 7)
  • Are the speakers on and getting signal? (steps 8–10)

Two parallel chains: mains and monitors

Almost everything on the board exists in two copies — one for the main mix (what the congregation hears) and one for the monitor mix (what the band hears on stage).

That’s why every channel has an AUX send (or several): the AUX is the “send some of this channel to the monitor.” The fader is the “send some of this channel to the main mix.”

When a singer says “I can’t hear myself in my monitor,” you change their AUX send, not their fader. When the room is too loud, you change the master fader, not the AUX.

Why this matters

Almost every “weird” sound problem becomes obvious once you ask “where in the chain?” Cable problems happen at step 3. Phantom power problems happen at step 4. Feedback happens because step 10 leaks back into step 2 in a loop. Clipping happens at step 4 when TRIM is too high.

If you remember nothing else, remember the order — and remember that monitors and mains are separate.

Suggestions on this site are guidance, not professional advice. If you are unsure, stop and ask an experienced sound engineer.
